utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Please be seated. Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Appearances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Nicholas Koumjian and Ann Sutherland, assisted by Ruth Karper for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Branko Lukic with Mr. John Ostojic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Any obstacles before we start?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We have the exhibits from the last witness first.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution seeks to tender exhibits premarked S119, S120, S121.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I suggest that we do this entire from together with list 2 and 3, after we have heard Witness, not to lose any time, and to be on the safe side that we really can conclude this witness this week. Thank you for the understanding.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: My understanding was that the actual witness is in open session, no protective measure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then Mr. Beglerbegovic be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Beglerbegovic. You can understand me? Thank you. Could you please give us the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Start the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, would you please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Ibrahim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And your family name?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Beglerbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Dr. Beglerbegovic, can you tell the Court the year that you were born.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I was born in 1946.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Where were you born? Where did you grow up?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I was born and I grew up in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us what your --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, we are getting the French translation on the English channel. At least, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sorry for the delay, Doctor. Minor technical problem. Doctor, can you tell the Court what your education was. Where were you educated, and in what field?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I finished primary and secondary school in Prijedor and the medical faculty in Zagreb. I specialised physical medicine in Zagreb in 1985. I finished my university in 1971.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: After finishing university and during your medical studies, did you begin to practice medicine in the municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: After finishing, yes, I got a job in Prijedor municipality, and at first I worked at the health centre in Prijedor. And after I returned from the army, I got a job at the health station in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you give us the years that you worked at the health station in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I started working there in 1973, in the spring of 1973. And I worked there for nearly ten years, until the beginning of 1983.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: After leaving that position in Omarska, where did you work?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I finished my specialisation, and I found a job in the Prijedor hospital, department of physical medicine and rehabilitation, which was one of the departments at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So in 1992, beginning of the year, where were you working and what was your position?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: In 1992, I was still working at the Prijedor hospital. I was head of the physical medicine and rehabilitation department in the Prijedor hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Was that hospital part of a bigger centre or complex?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The hospital was part of the medical centre of Prijedor. The name of the centre was Mladen Stojanovic. Mladen Stojanovic was a partisan doctor from World War II. Within the medical centre, there were also health centres, pharmacies, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Where did you -- what neighbourhood, without giving me the address, but what neighbourhood did you live in the beginning of 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I lived nearly plumb in the centre of Prijedor, and that part of town was called Local Commune Prijedor 2, and there was the neighbourhood of Puharska also very close, but actually where I lived was closer to the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps we could have S3, the town map, put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, the usher is preparing a map that will be on our videoscreens, but I would like, if possible, for you to actually look at the map on your right. And if you could -- you have a pointer there. If you could point to the general area where your house was and where the hospital was that you worked at. One moment, please. It's not quite ready yet. We're not getting an image. We're getting the doctor's tie at the moment on the screen. I think the mirror is not focussed on the map.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: The map is a bit small, but I hope I can point out everything. Approximately here, this is where my house was. It was beside the railway to Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: For the record, the witness indicated in the centre of the map, just above what appears to be the railway line running diagonally across the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You indicated where you lived. Where was the hospital?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: The hospital was here. Excuse me, no, it was here in this place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: While we're with the map, can you tell us, how far away from your house is the Keraterm camp? Where would that be in relation to the map?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure about how big the map is, but I think it must have been less than a kilometre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: From your house?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. We're done with the map. Thank you. As a medical doctor in Prijedor, did you know of a Dr. Stakic, Milomir Stakic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did know each other. He was younger than I was. But after I quit the job in Omarska, he came to work there, and we did meet several times. I believe that he knew me before I knew him, but yes, we did know each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you know about Dr. Stakic? Do you know where he was from?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. He's from the village of Maricka, close to Omarska, and it belongs to the Omarska district. When he was a young doctor, he came to the health centre in Omarska after I left. I didn't know a lot about him, not earlier at any rate. We did not have any contacts earlier. We belonged to different generations. Probably he studied elsewhere. I studied in Zagreb, so there wasn't really an opportunity for us to meet because we didn't live in the same area. So our paths never crossed except after he had become a doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The medical community in Prijedor, would you describe it as -- was it common for doctors to know each other or know of each other?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was common. There were certain meetings to attend by all doctors, and younger doctors, by the very nature of their work, had to consult older colleagues. So sometimes they even sent their patients to specialised doctors. So that was also another way for them to meet their older colleagues. And aside from that, there were cases where conferences were organised by pharmaceutical companies selling different medicines. So sometimes at these conferences, after these conferences, we had cocktail parties, and that's where doctors would, perhaps were not directly connected in their daily work, had an opportunity to meet. So I believe we must have met at one of these conferences. I can't remember when exactly, but that seems quite likely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, can you tell us, were you a member of any political parties?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Just before the war, I was a member of the Communist Association of Yugoslavia. That is, of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Most people in Yugoslavia at that time, especially in Bosnia, most people who had jobs and were employed were members of the communist party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In the 1990 elections, that period of time, after the fall of communism and prior to and during the conflict that took place in Bosnia, were you a member of any political party during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. After the disintegration of the communist party, I did not join any political party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Following Dayton and the peace agreement in 1996, did you join or form any political party?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: In 1997, I was a refugee in Sanski Most. I found a job there and worked at the health centre in Sanski Most. There were many people from Prijedor there. And together with a group of people from Prijedor, we founded a branch of the Party for Bosnia and Herzegovina. I was one of the founding members.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Who were the other founding members of that party from Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: One of the better known ones was Muharem Murselovic, who is now the president of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly. Furthermore, there were other people, but their names are not so well known. I think his is the best known because he holds that sort of position. There was Sead Suljanovic, Adim Selimbegovic, Fuad Grozdanic and other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever run for any political office as a member of that party?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I was on the list, and I was appointed a delegate in the Prijedor Municipal Assembly in the 1997 elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Were you ever a member of the SDA party?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: No, I never was a member of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, are you aware of any political parties that the accused Dr. Milomir Stakic belonged to?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I remember that at the time of the campaign for the founding of new parties when people from other republics, from Serbia and from Croatia Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. came to Bosnia, once in the village of Nisevic close to Omarska, a party was founded. I can't remember what it was called. Whether it was called or radical or liberal or a combination of these two I can't remember. But the president of that party was the man named Guberina. And the head of the party for the area of Omarska was then Mr. Stakic. He was elected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know what role Dr. Stakic had in Prijedor in the 1990 elections, if he obtained any position?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the 1990 elections, the greatest number of seats in the Municipal Assembly in Prijedor was won by the SDA, and then the SDS came second, then the HDZ and several other parties with a minor number of votes. There was the Reformist Party founded by Ante Markovic and some other parties, too. At the moment when the elections took place, I'm not sure whether this gentleman was a member of the SDS, but I know that the way positions were distributed and the rule was that the party that wins the greatest number of votes should elect the president of the Municipal Assembly. And those who come second have the right to appoint the deputy president. Mr. Stakic was appointed president. I'm not sure what that meant, but he must have changed his allegiance, because I don't think that being the party in which he was he would have been appointed. The SDS requested that all the people in the leading positions be their members. I think the area that Mr. Stakic comes from is predominantly a Serb area, and according to some rules, that area was supposed to have a representative in the parliament, a position of power in Prijedor. I think he was -- he was a good choice because he was an intellectual. He was a gentleman. He had finished university, so he met their criteria for being appointed. And that's why they elected him to represent them, so he was elected the deputy president of the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know what other positions Dr. Stakic assumed in 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Apart from this position of deputy president, I can't remember anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know what positions Dr. Stakic took after the takeover on the 30th of April, 1992, of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: After the takeover in Prijedor, the so-called Crisis Staff was established which took over the functions of the legally elected assembly, because all the members of the assembly who were not Serbs were either expelled or thrown out. There was the so-called Serbian Municipality of Prijedor, and after the Serbian municipality was established, the Crisis Staff was established, headed by Mr. Stakic. Probably by virtue of his function in the Municipal Assembly, he was appointed as the president of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us during the events that you witnessed, that you live through in 1992, did you hear much about this Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Most of what was happening in the positions of power was on behalf of the Crisis Staff, whenever there was some sort of proclamation it was always by the Crisis Staff. If a rally was organised, if there was a warning, a public warning to the citizens. Most of the decisions that were made at that time, when the Crisis Staff was founded, came from the Crisis Staff or on behalf the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: During 1992, did you ever see Dr. Stakic mentioned in the media?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: There were a number of such cases in the newspapers, on TV, whenever something was happening, rallies, he was present by virtue of his position because he was the first man in Prijedor. It was logical for him to appear whenever these events were covered in the newspapers or on TV, the radio stations, of course, he was always there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you ever meet with Dr. Stakic after the conflict?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: After the conflict, I did meet him in Prijedor in 1996. I think it was February or March, I can't remember. But it was early 1996. I was one of the five members of the delegation that came from Sanski Most to Prijedor for negotiations as a delegation of the charitable society of Merhamet, whose member I was. And we came to talk to the Red Cross people from Prijedor in order to make contact. It was under the aegis of an international organisation. I can't remember which one, and they wanted this to be the initial attempt at rapprochement, and it was the first time after the Dayton agreements that anyone from Prijedor came back to Prijedor as a refugee from Prijedor. We met at the Municipal Assembly hall in Prijedor. I can't remember who were the members of his delegation. I remember that we shook hands. It was a very cold meeting. There was no warmth between us. I had the impression that they only decided to go ahead with this meeting because the international organisation that organised the meeting demanded that we meet. But I believe that if it hadn't been for the international organisation, this meeting would never have taken place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What was Dr. Stakic's position at that time, in early 1996, when you met him at the Prijedor Municipal Assembly building?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. We let the opposite side to have one question, but we think this is outside the scope of the indictment. So that's basically our objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Dismissed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You may answer, Doctor. Do you know what Dr. Stakic's position was in early 1996 when you met him?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: He was then the president of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Going back to 1992, you talked about seeing Dr. Stakic in the media and at public, or reported to be at public meetings. Did you make any observations about his attitude towards the SDS policies and what was going on in Prijedor at that time?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: There were certain occasions when leaders of the Republika Srpska came to Prijedor. The president Biljana Plavsic, Mr. Krajisnik, Karadzic. Before that, Karadzic was president, of course, and then Biljana Plavsic came. By virtue of his position, of course, he was the one who received them. He could be seen there, and I got the impression that he was happy to be in a position to receive these people in Prijedor, talk with them and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you recall the events of the 30th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Tell us when you became aware of what was going on and what your reaction was to it.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of what was going on for a very long time. Whatever was happening, I thought it was a short-term thing, something that would soon pass. And the same applies to the event on the 30th of April, 1992. I got up in the morning and I saw, in some very prominent places outside important institutions, outside companies, I saw Serb flags in certain spots along the road to the city. I saw armed guards, soldiers. They were IDing people who were passing by these checkpoints. And then I saw that something had happened that night. In a peaceful way, perhaps without a single bullet fired, a group of people probably led by the SDS toppled the government of Prijedor and proclaimed the Serbian Municipality of Prijedor. Those were the first signs of the changes that were taking place. Later people were fired from their jobs, Muslims, most of the Croats, too. In some companies more, in some with a certain amount of reserve, not unmasked like that but then increasingly so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You talked about checkpoints. Were you able to go to work that day after the takeover, and how did it affect your life? Were you able to continue working?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I was able to work, but I had to pass through a checkpoint at a crossroads between my house and the hospital, and also at the entrance to the hospital, although I had been working there for almost ten years. I started in 1985, so well, it wasn't ten, it was about seven years. All the porters knew me, everybody at the entrance knew me, but the porter still asked to see my ID card and looked at it before letting me in. So I was able to work but was subject to checks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: These checkpoints, could you tell who was manning the checkpoints or can you describe if they were wearing any uniforms or had weapons?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: The people manning the checkpoints wore uniforms of the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army, but the reservists, they wore olive-grey uniforms, which every reservist had at home in case a situation arose, an exercise or something worse. And they were wearing those uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Was it possible for you, in any way, to tell the ethnicity of the people that were manning the checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, those people I knew, if I knew who they were, then I could see that those people were Serbs. I don't remember seeing any Muslims or Croats at a checkpoint or wearing the uniform at that time. I'm not claiming that there weren't any others, but mostly they were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You mentioned that people were dismissed from their positions. Let's start first with your position as head of the department. Can you tell us, did you maintain that position throughout 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: No. I continued working, but very soon the director handed me a decision which told me I was no longer the head of the service for physical medicine and rehabilitation of the hospital in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you remember approximately when that was?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: It might have been around, well, in the first ten days of June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You said that the hospital was part of a centre. Was there a director of the hospital, separate from a director of the centre?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was the general director of the medical centre. That was one person. And there was another person who was the director of the hospital which was part of the medical centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'd like the witness -- who was the director of the centre?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: At the time of these events, the director of the medical centre in Prijedor was Risto Banovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When you say "at the time of these events," are you speaking of at least before the 30th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so. Before April 1992, and immediately after that, but only for a brief time. Very soon, he was replaced.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What was the education of Mr. Banovic or Dr. Banovic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: He was not a doctor; he was a psychologist. He graduated in psychology, but he had a university degree, and he was a psychologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Who was he replaced by?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: He was replaced by Ranko Sikman, who was a senior technician, a man of far less education, but he was appointed there at the orders of the SDS, as an SDS member.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Banovic was of Serb ethnicity. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Banovic was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know if Mr. Banovic was a member of the SDS or some other political party?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Banovic was not a member of the SDS. He was in the SDP, which remained after the communist party fell apart. It was called the Social Democrat Party or something like that. Anyway, it was the SDP, and he was a member of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know, was Mr. Banovic an active or high-profile member of the SDP?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't say he was very active or high-profile member. He was better known as a citizen and as the director of the hospital than as a member of that party. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like the witness to be shown S86. And for the record, again, this is a document that indicates in the letterhead: "The Crisis Staff and the war presidency of the Prijedor municipality, Municipal Assembly of Prijedor, Prijedor. Subject: Action upon the objections submitted by the Omarska club of deputies." And the signature line on the second page indicates: "Crisis Staff, war presidency," with no handwriting. But the very last lines indicates "decisions on dismissals and appointments were published in the official gazette of the Prijedor municipality, number 292, with 25 June, 1992 on the with names included as above." If the witness could be shown 86B, the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would you please also provide us with the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: It's 65 ter number 299.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We have two extra copies if it would be helpful to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Is that exhibit on the list we received?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Ms. Karper indicates she called today. I just found this actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The Defence has a copy of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Dr. Beglerbegovic, directing your attention to the first point of these 17 numbered points, it indicates "Ranko Sikman has been appointed acting director of the MC, replacing Risto Banovic." Are these the two individuals that you just described to us?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm finished with that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, were more people in the hospital dismissed besides Mr. Sikman?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: You mean Risto. There's a slight misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sorry. Excuse me. Mr. Banovic.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I have already said quite a lot of people were dismissed. That applies to the hospital, too. But after the attack on Prijedor on the 25th of May, 1992, there was a large number of dismissals, mostly of Muslims and Croats, because of the fighting and because communications were cut off, especially for people commuting from outside town and they were simply unable to go to work. This was taken as grounds for dismissal. And in many decisions issued at the time, it is stated that failure to report to work was the reason for the dismissal. And the decisions always refer to the decision issued by the Crisis Staff of the Prijedor Municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Who was the director of the hospital before the takeover?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Before the takeover of power, Dr. Nikola Tesinic, who was an eye specialist, was the director of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: He was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know if he was a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I think he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Who replaced Mr. Tesinic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Tesinic was replaced by Dr. Radojka Elenkov, a specialist in internal medicine who worked at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know if this doctor was an SDS member?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but I think she was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, were you married at this time?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Was your wife also a Bosniak? Excuse me, I haven't asked you that question yet, so I should first ask you. What is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What is your wife's ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: My wife is also a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us, what was your wife's position before the takeover?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: My wife graduated in pharmacy, and she was the director of the pharmacy organisation covering all the pharmacists in the area of Prijedor that belonged to the medical centre. It was a so-called basic organisation of associated labour. This was a remnant from the former system, but that was its name. And within this organisation, there were three pharmacies in Prijedor, a pharmacy in Sanski Most, one in Omarska, one in Kozarac, and one in Bosanski Novi. There was a director responsible for all those pharmacies, and my wife was the director at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Was Prijedor considered to be the centre of that regional organisation?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What happened to your wife regarding her position after the takeover?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: My wife, from the 1st of June, 1992, was told orally that it would be better for her not to come to work until the situation calmed down. And she and all the other women working in the pharmaceutical division who were women who were Bosniaks, they stopped going to work because without any written decision or anything in writing, they were simply told by word of mouth not to report for work any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did she continue to receive any salary?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember. I think that maybe in the first month she was even on the payroll, but she didn't want to go and receive the money because she was proud. And she was hurt that she had been told not to go to work. So she refused to take that salary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you have a brother who was working in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had an older brother who was an economist by profession. And at the time of these events in 1992, he was the director of a building construction company called Mrakovica Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did your brother maintain his position after the takeover?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: No. The list of 17 people that was shown recently also contains the name of my brother, Janko Stjepic, who was dismissed [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May we, in addition, ask the first name of your wife, please, for the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sadeta Beglerbegovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And Rizah Beglerbegovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's my brother.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And that's a person on the document we just saw, number 15. Right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. Would Your Honour like that put before the witness again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Giro Mrakovica instead of Beglerbegovic, Rizah, Janko Stjepic is appointed director.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: On the 1st of July, 1992, did you go to work?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the 1st of July, 1992, I went to work as I did every morning. And I had to show my identity card at the entrance. After that, I went through the security check, and I went to my workplace, although on that day, a large number of Muslims, or Bosniaks, who had not been dismissed on the 1st of June were dismissed on that day. I met my colleague, a senior therapist, a Bosniak, who was told to go home. He was told not to work any more. And he was surprised to see that I had gone through the security check, because under the same criteria, I, too, was supposed to stop working. Probably at the moment I was at the checkpoint, the former director or even the then director, but I think it was the former director, Mr. Tesinic, the doctor I have mentioned, and the people who are doing the checks respected him. So maybe that's why they made the mistake and let me through. I learned that at 10.00 a.m. when we had our break, and there were very few patients there at the time, at least in my ward, because we don't have any emergency cases in that ward. Suddenly, I heard military boots coming down the corridor in the direction of my office. A reserve policeman entered the office. He was not an active but a reserve policeman. He was wearing a camouflage uniform which was a blue camouflage uniform of the kind worn by policemen, distinct from the kind worn by soldiers, so you could tell reserve policemen apart from reserve soldiers because of the colour of the camouflage uniform. And he addressed me very rudely and said: "What are you doing here?" I was surprised, and I said: "Why are you asking me what I'm doing here? This is where I work." And he said to me: "You don't work here any more. Get your things together and go home." So what else could I do? I gathered up my belongings, and I went home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you ever receive any formal document regarding your dismissal?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: No. I never got any kind of document in writing, either then or later. Later on, I learned that I had been removed from work, not permanently, but that I was on what they called standby, that's what they called it when people were sent home because there was not enough work. They were not dismissed, but they were put on standby, and they were obliged to report every so often. I was told to report to the management or the administration of the hospital in Prijedor every 15 days, which I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the Court's permission, I'd like to show the witness two documents, 65 ter numbers 477 and 478. There is, at the moment, no translation. The documents, I believe, are identical except for the blanks that are typewritten in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could the witness be so kind and read out one document that we have access to the contents of the document. I believe, indeed, it is at least similar, the second document. So it's only necessary to have one document in the transcript. Would you please be so kind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It says in the heading: "Work organisation, Medical Centre, Dr. Mladen Stojanovic, Prijedor. Dr. Mladen Stojanovic, Prijedor. Basic Organisation of Associated Labour. Working community. General hospital. Prijedor. Number 02674/1. Date: The 25th of May, 1992. "Pursuant to Article 75, paragraph 2, item 3 of the law on the basic rights stemming from employment, and in connection with with the conclusions of the Crisis Staff of the Prijedor Municipality number 02111-132/92 of the 5th of June, 1992, I hereby issue a decision on the termination of employment. "One, to the employee, Dr. Majda Sadikovic, who is at the post of a person doing her specialisation, in the organisational unit of anaesthesia and intensive care, whose employment is to be terminated on the 25th of May, 1992 because of unauthorised absence from work at the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. time of a work obligation. "Number two, on the day when her employment is terminated, the above-named loses all her rights stemming from employment. "Grounds or statement of reasons: On the basis of the general mobilisation on the territory of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, work obligation has been introduced in the working organisation, Dr. Mladen Stojanovic medical centre Prijedor for all employees, starting from the 25th of May, 1992. The Crisis Staff of the Prijedor Municipality, at its session held on the 5th of June, 1992, issued a conclusion whereby all directors of basic organisations of associated labour shall, for workers or employees who have not responded to the work obligation, they shall dismiss them from work. "The law on the basic rights stemming from employment, Article 75, paragraph 2, item 3, prescribes that an employee's employment shall be terminated without the agreement of the employee, if he's absent from work without justification for five working days. As the above-named employee has not responded to the work obligation in the -- within the deadline mentioned above, all the above-mentioned conditions for the issuing of a decision on the termination of employment have been met. "Legal remedy: The employee has the right to complain to the Workers' Council of the Basic Organisation of Associated Labour within 15 days of the date of receipt of this decision. "Delivered to the above-named, to the acting director, to the personnel service, to the archives, acting director of the basic organisation of associated labour, the working organisation, Dr. Radojka Elenkov, specialist of internal medicine."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Do you know Dr. Majda Sadikovic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Not very well. But yes, I was acquainted with her.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What was her ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Muslim, Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Referring to the next document, do you know Dr. Mirsad Osmanovic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know him, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: He was also a Muslim, a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour. Did we give these an S number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No. Not yet. Correct me if I am wrong, 477 should go as S124B. And it should be added to the record that a translation of the basic text can be found on page 21 of the transcript of 6 June 2002. And Document 478 should go as S125B. And the translation can be found on the transcript of 6 June, 2002, page 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just to conclude this point, are there any objections as to the admission into evidence of these two documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence under these two numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm done with these documents and am prepared to move into a new area if you'd like to take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Come back to the third document that you have for today. That would be in the context.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: That will come up later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Then the trial stands adjourned until 15.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. And please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, sometime in May of 1992, did you hear an announcement regarding surrendering of weapons?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was an announcement outside the Crisis Staff that all those who were in possession of weapons, legally or illegally owned weapons, should turn in their weapons at a determined place at a determined time. The deadline was the day before the attack. I can't remember, the 24th or the 25th of May. It was Saturday. The attack took place on Saturday. That was the last deadline for the weapons to be turned in. I was in possession of a legally owned pistol, and I was getting ready to turn it in at the police station where we were supposed to turn in our weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What did you do with your pistol?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I didn't turn it in eventually, because early in the morning the attack was launched and it wasn't possible to go to the centre or to the police station. There was shooting for the whole morning. So I couldn't go, but members of the army, who were in my street, came into my house, searched the house, and took the pistol. So I didn't turn it in where I was supposed to turn it in, but it was taken from me, with no written certificate. One of the soldiers just took it and left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When you talk about an attack and shooting, are you talking about shooting in the town of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, probably, because we could hear it very clearly when the shooting began. I didn't know exactly where, but it appeared to have come from the bridge on the Sana, and I later found out that most of the shooting took place there. But at that moment I couldn't tell because I was staying quite far from that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: There's a little confusion perhaps because I'm not sure which event you're talking about. Are you talking about, as far as you know, an attack upon Prijedor from non-Serbs, from mainly Muslims?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I wonder to make the transcript clearer if we can agree with Defence counsel on the correct date for that event. Your Honours, I propose that the parties agree that the event in question, what we have been referring to during this trial as the attack on Prijedor was the 30th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We stipulate to that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The Prosecution agrees to that fact also, stipulates to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for these agreed facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, we recognise that you don't carry a calendar for 1992, or diary with you. That event occurred on the 30th of May, the attack on Prijedor the town by the Muslim forces. The announcement that you're talking about, when did that occur in relation to that attack on the 30th of May?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: The announcement was published before that event. That was earlier, but I must have confused the dates. The 24th and the 25th was the attack on Kozarac, by a different army. So this may be a mistake that I made. But the announcement was given before the attack of, as you have just said, the non-Serb forces on Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just so we're clear, and tell us if you're not sure, is the announcement you're talking about, did it occur before the attack by the non-Serb forces on the 30th of May, or before the attack on Kozarac on the 24th of May? Do you recall which event this announcement preceded? And if you're not sure, say so. What's your best recollection now?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I can't say with any degree of certainty, but the announcement did not refer to one day only. Maybe it was there for several days. But as far as I can remember, the last deadline for turning in the weapons was a Saturday, and I wanted to turn in my pistol on that Saturday. But that was the day the attack began.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: After the attack on the town which we've agreed is the 30th of May, was there some announcement by the authorities regarding -- I'm sorry, perhaps I can stop for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I don't know if anyone has the calendar for 1992. We believe that the 24th of May is a Sunday. Perhaps later we can stipulate to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's come back to this after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sorry, Doctor. Going back, after the attack on Prijedor by the non-Serb forces, was there an announcement regarding the safety of Muslims in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: For the whole day, when the shooting stopped and when the situation calmed down in a way, on Radio Prijedor there were announcements. They explained, they exhorted, and one such announcement that got me really worried at that moment was an announcement requesting all the citizens of Prijedor to recognise the authorities. But they said at the end of the announcement that the safety of the Muslims was not guaranteed. I was afraid that someone would just simply come over to my house and kill me, and my wife and my children were also in the house. But this really remains clear in my memory. At the end of the announcement, they said that the safety of the Muslims was not guaranteed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: At that time, was there a further announcement regarding non-Serbs marking their houses, identifying their houses in some way?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. On that day, members of the Serbian army ordered all Muslims to hang a white flag on their houses, or something resembling a white flag, a blanket or a towel, a white towel. It was compulsory to mark all these houses with a white flag, a piece of cloth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: At that time, back in late May of 1992, what was your reaction to an announcement like that for Muslims to mark their houses?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: As everyone else, I was afraid that something would happen because in their explanation, they said whoever failed to do this, their houses would be shelled because there were tanks in the town. I saw two tanks passing by. And they said: "Whoever fails to put out a white flag, their houses will be shelled." I saw that all my neighbours had done it, so I put one up, too, a big white towel, sort of like a flag.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: After the takeover on the 30th of April and leading up to the summer of 1992, did you become aware of any arrests of non-Serb citizens in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were arrests. But most of the arrests started taking place after the attack, after the 30th of May. There were sporadic arrests earlier, too, but not in such a drastic measure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: At some time, did you become aware of camps where non-Serbs were detained in the municipality of Prijedor? And excuse me, we've talked about this, I believe, you and I in the last few days. If you feel you come to a point where you need to give us confidential information that should not be public, please so indicate. And before you do so, and we will go into private session.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I learned about the camps from other people's accounts, but I also had a source, another source, that unless I have to, I would not disclose publicly. This source told me about the camp, what was happening there, what the conditions were like, how people lived in the camp and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I don't need the name, but if Your Honours or the Defence does, then we can go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's please go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Confirmed. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What did this person tell you about what was happening at the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: He told me that the situation was very bad over there, that it was overcrowded, that the living conditions were awful, that they slept on the floor, on cement, on the tiles, that the hygiene facilities were minimal, that food rations were distributed once a day only, usually consisting of some sort of soup, just water heated up, so to say, that the prisoners were being beaten and killed, and that the estimate was that they would all eventually be killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did that worry you for a particular reason?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: It did worry me very much because at the time he gave me this information, my brother was already in the camp. So at that moment, it didn't even occur to me that I myself might end up there, too, but I was very much afraid for his sake because he was already there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: This is the brother that you mentioned earlier who was the director of the construction company?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I only have one brother, and he is this person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Was your brother married, and if so, what was the ethnicity of his wife?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: He was married, and his wife was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did your brother have any political -- was he involved in politics at all prior to his arrest?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was. He was a member of the Reformist Party led by Ante Markovic. He was the deputy president of the party for Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did he hold any elected position?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: As a member of the party, he was appointed a delegate to the Prijedor Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you know other people who had been arrested and taken to camps, or as far as you know were arrested and taken away?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, man people were arrested. I know that the now president of the Municipal Assembly, Muhamed Cehajic, had been arrested, and the director of the -- the director of the cookies factory, who was a Croat by ethnicity, was also arrested. A lawyer, the president of the Prijedor HDZ, Saric Silvije was also arrested. I just remembered their names now, but there were other people, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You mentioned that you heard about the camps from other people besides this source. In your opinion, was it common knowledge at that time that there were camps in Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: News spread very soon about camps being set up, because the relatives and acquaintances of the people who were already in the camp knew about the camps. They knew that the camp had been established and that it was in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: On the 6th of July, what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: The 6th of July, 1992, around 2.00 in the afternoon, a car with civilian license plates, a Mercedes pulled up, and a policeman came out, an active-duty policeman from the Prijedor police station. Bato Kovacevic. I was in my garden. It was summer, so I was only wearing my swimsuit. He knew me, and he spoke to me. He said: "Doctor, get ready, you're coming with me." I knew that Bato had already taken many people away and taken them for an interview like he came for me, and I knew that it was now my turn. I asked him what I should put on. I was a bit clumsy with these things. I didn't know what to wear, and he told me: "This will all be over very soon. You're just coming for an interview, but it won't take long." I put on some light clothes. He took me there in a car, and there was another policeman with us. I think his name was Zrnic, but I'm not sure. He took me to the police station. We went into one of the rooms there. Waiting for us there was a man I knew, a Serb policeman. He was very cold, and he didn't show that he knew me. After a couple of minutes, I sat down, and the man who brought me there came in. He asked: "What shall we do with him?" as if he had gone out of the room to ask, to consult, one of his superiors as to do with me, and he came back after a while and said: "We'll do the same thing as we did to the previous one." I was taken out of the office then through the garden to another room which had an iron door. It was dark, no windows. 3 times 3 metres. I went in. It was dark. And it was difficult to adapt to darkness. I couldn't see anything. Where there was supposed to be a window, there was only a piece of tin, perforated, very small holes that allowed some light in, but that was very difficult for a man who just walked in from outside, from sunlight, to see anything in that room. I found there another two or three people who sat on some sort of a wooden board inside the room. There was only a soldiers' blanket on that board. And in the corner behind the door, something stank. I realised later on that they used the corner for a toilet because there was no toilet there. I spent about two hours there, talking to the people who were there. We discussed all sorts of things, that you do in the circumstances, why did they bring you in, why did they bring me in. After about two hours, a paddy wagon came along. They took me and another person out. The other person's name was Idriz Jakupovic. And inside the wagon there was already one person. He took his from his home. His name was Ibrahim Mujkanovic. They shut the door of the paddy wagon, and we went somewhere. I know the town. I know where the police station was, and where the camps were. They didn't tell us where we were headed, but we knew that we were headed for one of the camps. I tried to reconstruct the route in my head, according to how long the drive was. And I couldn't see, but I knew that we had passed Keraterm already because that would only have been a very short drive. This meant that we were going to Omarska. And the drive from Prijedor to Omarska takes about half an hour. We took the main road. I was very interested in seeing what it was like in Kozarac, because houses had been burned there. And a lot had been destroyed, but I couldn't see it from the car, from the paddy wagon. We reached Omarska late in the afternoon, early evening. It was a hot summer day. The driver opened the door, and we saw a large number of people, lying on the ground. I didn't know then that this piece of ground was called pista. It was outside a big hangar in Omarska. Some people sat on the ground and some people lay on the ground. One of the people who came with me was very impressed by what he saw, and his reaction was: "Where did all these people come from?" That was his reaction. "What's all this about?" After the reception procedure, and we were received by policemen, Mlado Radic, Krkan, who was on duty then. I knew him personally, and he knew me, because I worked for years in Omarska and we attended a number of meetings and rallies together even before the war. He verbally abused me and he said: "Hey, Doctor, what are you doing here?" Because he was apparently surprised that I was there. And I said: "Well, what do you think, I just came by myself to have a look?" So their reception procedure also consisted of searching us for weapons. And to go through all the checks and reach the camp with some weapons on was an absurd idea, but they still searched us because the rules said they should. They wanted us to put our hands in the air and show three fingers like this lined up as we were against the wall as they were feeling us for weapons. Knowing this policeman, I just put all five fingers in the air, not three as we were required to do. Someone with a very rough voice behind my back said: "You, fatso, you too, get your hands up in the air." I don't know why, but that was a rule apparently. I wouldn't like to make any further comments now, but we were supposed to lift up in the air three fingers. It's a special sign, someone who does not belong to the community that uses this sign should not be made to do this, but I won't comment on this now. After that, we were taken to the garage. It's a very famous place in the Omarska camp. The garage is big enough to hold two big expensive cars. It has an iron door. I found there about 70 people crammed in that space. I'm not sure if I'm speaking too comprehensively. Should I go into further details? Be that as it may, when I came in, what I saw was just dreadful. There was a group of people inside who had been transferred from the Keraterm camp to the Omarska camp on that day. They originally came from the Ljubija area and from the villages around area. There were a lot of Muslims, but also Croats because that area has a lot of Croat villages. Those people were beaten black and blue. They moaned. All the clothes they had on them, they used to make bandages. They had all sorts of bruises of all sizes all over their bodies. And I could even see a shoe mark on the body of one of them, a soldier's boot, the same mark it leaves when pressed against fresh snow. They were lined up that morning when they were brought in. I didn't see this myself but I was told what happened to them. They lined them up in two rows against the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. garage wall with their faces against the wall and they were beating them from the back with rods. They were kicking them. They used whatever they could, and you could see the results. You could see the traces on most of these people. What else could I say about this room? It was stuffy. People were lying on the floor. I can't remember if it was cement or ceramic tiles. Some people found pieces of cardboard to lie on, and some people used plastic. There was a tin container beside the door that was used as a toilet because there was no toilet. And half a metre from this tin container, the first prisoner was lying, and then they were all lying one next to another in that garage. I found a place for myself to lie, and I spent the night there. Some of the people there knew me, some of the guards, too. So they just come over to see me. I didn't enjoy any privileges, but I could tell that even some of them were not exactly sure why I had been brought in. I could tell by their faces, but also I could tell there was nothing they could do about it or change it. The only change was that the next day, I was moved from the garage to the so-called glass house, in the part of the camp that was close to the kitchen. From the accounts of other prisoners, people who were put in the glass house were considered to be slightly privileged, perhaps they bribed someone or perhaps they were just well-respected citizens. But I saw there a number of intellectuals and well-respected people. There were a couple of Serbs there, too, two Serbs who must have done something wrong so they were put there, too. I spent that night in the glass house. And from the glass house, I could see that evening the arrival of other people who were being brought to the camp. They were made to enter the camp one by one, in silence. There was a large number of people being brought in. I couldn't tell exactly where, but they came the same way that they used to go to get their food. So there were several rows of these people, and the room was filled with rows, lines, of people standing next to one another. So there is no way to take up physically less space than this, and then people were ordered to lie down, and then there would be havoc because people started pushing and shoving. So that also left a deep impression on me. Sometimes it would happen that people spent -- slept outside, and sometimes it would rain. Not that night, however. It was quite warm, and I think most of these people would have been better off staying outside for the night but they were still crammed into that room. I could also see people queuing up for their food from the glass house. They came in groups of 30, not more. The kitchen, I think, could hold at least 300 people because there were as many tables there in the kitchen. But they apparently had their own rules and just split the prisoners up into groups of 30, because that way it was easier for them to control people on the way in. And every day, they would beat people on the way in. Some people were starved, some people were sick, so they walked slowly, and they floundered because they couldn't walk normally. But whoever halted and whoever walks slowly would be beaten. There was a man, I didn't know his name, he was completely disoriented. He didn't know where he was. And none of the people who brought him there were able to help him. And the guards really took it out on him. And they beat him black and blue. He could hardly stand up. I said before what food rations were like, it was warm soup with maybe a leaf of cabbage in it. The meal lasted for a short time, maybe 2 or 3 minutes, and then we were ordered to go out. Most of the people barely managed to drink some of the contents. People were given one eighth usually of a loaf of bread, and they would all be chased out and another group brought in. There were other things about this kitchen. There were women there in the corner also who just stood there and watched. Some of them helped with the distribution of food rations, but most of them just sat by and watched these scenes. The next day, when I got up in the morning, I was in the glass house, I saw Zeljko Meakic, who was the commander of the camp. He was wearing a uniform, and he gave a sign. He beckoned me through the glass to come out, and then I came out. And he said: "I have good news for you. 98 per cent -- it is 98 per cent certain that you will be released and go home. And as for the 2 per cent of uncertainty, wait until I come back from Prijedor." Which means that he had been told that I was to be released but he had to go to Prijedor to doublecheck. So that's how he explained the situation to me. Of course, I was glad to learn this, and I believed that my release was quite likely. I was immediately in a better mood. And then in the afternoon, he came back to tell me that I was free to go home and I was released on the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. I'd like to now go over a few details about what you told us. The police station that you were taken to, was that the SUP building, SUP, in Prijedor town?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was the building of the SUP, right next to the Municipal Assembly building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You said that you were taken in a wagon to Omarska with two other people. I believe you said their names were Idriz Jakupovic and Ibrahim Okanovic [Realtime transcript read in error "Mujkanovic"]. Can you tell us, who was Idriz Jakupovic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Idriz Jakupovic was the director of the social welfare centre in Prijedor, the centre for social work. There is a mistake here. Ibrahim's name was Okanovic, not Mujkanovic. There's an error in the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The transcript you see in front of you is not the final one, so do not be too concerned with spelling errors. But thank you. Who was Ibrahim Okanovic? How did he get to be in Prijedor that day?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Ibrahim Okanovic was a citizen of Prijedor, who just before these events in early 1992 left for Australia. He played football before the war, and when he got older, he became a football coach in Prijedor and the vicinity, and he went to Australia. I don't know what the circumstances were, and he settled there, and even found a football club where he became the coach. In April 1992, his father died. Maybe it was a bit earlier. I'm not sure. But he didn't manage to attend his father's funeral, but felt obliged to visit his father's grave. He arrived just before the events in Prijedor, and then the borders were closed, and he was unable to leave again. So he remained in Prijedor, and probably because -- well, I don't know why, but he was arrested, like many others. He was arrested on that day and taken to Omarska. Later on, nothing was known about him or Idriz Jakupovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You say "nothing was known about him..." Do you have any information about their fate, whether they survived Omarska?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, when you say that nothing is known about someone who was in Omarska, it's almost certain that they are dead. They were probably killed and buried, but the gravesite is not known because nobody has been found alive who went missing in Omarska, at least not so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You described to us having to place three fingers up against the wall. And you indicated that that was a sign of a particular group. Is it correct that that is a sign of Serb nationalist symbol, the three-finger salute?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: It was used as a nationalist symbol at the time. I think it's a symbol that deserves respect, because it's a symbol of the orthodox faith It symbolises the holy trinity. I am not well educated in religious matters, but I think it's something sacred for orthodox Serbs. But making a Muslim prisoner make the sign, I think, is sacrilege. It's an abuse of the sign. But it did have nationalist overtones at the time, although I didn't think it should be understood in that way, in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. When you were in the Omarska camp, is it correct from what you've told us that you spent only two nights at the camp. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: During those two nights, and at least part of three days, did you ever see any corpses in the camp?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: On the next morning when I woke up in the glass house, I was able to see the white house from there. That's another part of the Omarska camp. And next to the white house, there were four or five corpses in the grass. I was looking from the glass house, and the white house was on the right-hand side. And to the left of it, there were four or five corpses. And some of the people who had been in the glass house from before told me that these people had been killed on the previous night and put there that morning. It was too far for me to see who they were, but I could see four or five corpses. I can't tell you the exact number, but that's what I saw. A man who arrived in the glass house before me explained this to me. We could see the same scene every morning, sometimes there were more corpses, sometimes less, but in any case, that's what I saw that morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you see the corpses disposed of?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: The corpses were disposed of, but I did not see it being done. After a certain time, they were no longer there, so somebody had removed them. I heard that it was prisoners who removed the corpses, that they were used to pick up the corpses and put them on the vehicles they were taken away in. But I only heard that. I didn't see it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, you had mentioned in the beginning of your testimony having worked ten years in the Omarska area. At the camp, did you feel that there were many people in authority there that you knew?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No, sorry. Were there people running the camp that knew you from your time in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you know the commander of the camp?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, if we go from the top, I knew Zeljko Meakic, the camp commander, well, and he knew me well. We were often together. I was the director of the health centre which was later renamed, and by the nature of our work, we attended certain meetings that had to be attended by leading people in various organisations and institutions in the town. We also met at events such as weddings or celebrations, and also orthodox feasts in the villages. Every family has a certain feast day that they celebrate and we would meet at those celebrations. I also knew Miroslav Kvocka who was his deputy. I knew many of the guards, Radic, Krkan, Gruban, Ckalja. I knew many guards who were not guard shift leaders but ordinary guards. The only people I didn't know were younger people who had arrived before I was there, but yes, most of them knew me and I knew them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, did you get an impression from speaking to other prisoners perhaps, or from other sources that your release from the camp was a normal or unusual event? What was your impression?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, but up until the time I was released, I don't know that anyone was released. If there were any such people, it was a very small number. I am one of the few who arrived in the camp but was released before the camp was closed down. It's possible. I'm not claiming that there was no one, but if there were such people, it was a very small or negligible number. When I was released, it was a sign of hope for the other prisoners. They hoped that there was a change coming, a kind of thaw, and that others would also be released. People became a little more optimistic and started believing that things were getting better. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you see your brother at the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did see him. Let me tell you. I had a relative freedom of movement because I knew the guards, and they did not treat me cruelly. I was allowed to have contact with my brother and others. For example, Dr. Eso Sadikovic, a colleague of mine who was already in the camp, so I did have this opportunity, and I have to say that I was privileged in relation to other prisoners because I was allowed to have contact with my brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When you -- when Meakic indicated to you that you would be released, did you ask him about your brother? Can you briefly explain?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When Meakic arrived with this news from Prijedor that a definite decision had been reached to release me, the word went round, and a group of people from Omarska, who were not guards but simply residents of Omarska who knew me from before, arrived in the camp wishing to take me away because the news spread very quickly through the village, through the neighbourhood. And we sat next to a wall in the shade behind the kitchen near the entrance where food was brought in. There was some nice shade there, and we sat down and had some beer. And this was unprecedented for a prisoner to drink beer. But I was no longer officially a prisoner. My brother was also brought there and we sat down together and had some beer. So I addressed Meakic on that occasion and said: "There's something I'd like to ask you." He said: "Don't ask me to release your brother." Well, to be quite honest, I didn't even dream of asking him that. I was a little more naive. And I was only going to ask for my brother to be put in a better room, because he was in Mujo's room or Burho's room which was very uncomfortable. It was very, very crowded, and in the glass house where I had spent the second night, it was quite pleasant because part of it was open. You could see the open sky, but people slept under a roof, so that even if it rained people wouldn't get wet, but they still had a lot of fresh air. The glass house was built so as to have more light and air in the dining room. I asked him to put my brother in the place that was now vacant because I had been released. I wanted to get better conditions for my brother. But later on, I realised I had been very naive. He did indeed grant my wish, and my brother was moved to the glass house. But there, he was more exposed to view, and there was more possibility for him to be taken out, for his name to be called out. It was like a shop window. Everyone could be seen, and it was very risky being there because you were a target. And whenever they wanted to, for any reason, I don't know what the reasons were, they would take people out to be beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Tell us what happened when you were released. Did you go directly home or did you have to get some paperwork?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I have already said that my acquaintances from Omarska turned up and wanted to take me away in their private car. But they were told that this was out of the question, and that I was to be taken back in an official vehicle just as I had been brought in. And I was taken away in a small van, which was used to bring investigators in from Prijedor. These were people who interrogated the prisoners. I went back with them, and I was taken to the police station again to be issued with a document saying that I had been released from the camp and I was to keep this for my own security and for my movement through the town. It was summertime, and it was still light at 8.00 in the evening. Inspector Mijic was in charge of issuing this document to me. Of course, he addressed me very formally. He told me to sit and wait. I waited for an hour. Nobody came to get me. I was sitting in a kind of lobby. People were going in and out. They were well-built young men wearing camouflage uniforms. Some even had leather jackets. They were wearing gloves with the fingers cut off, and there were some men whom I didn't know, but fortunately they didn't know me either so they paid no attention to me. At one point, the duty officer approached me, and he was from Prijedor and knew who I was, and he hadn't seen me there before. And he approached me and said: "What are you doing here?" And I said: "I've come from the camp, I'm waiting." And he said: "Get out of here, get out of here." He took me to a room, he said: "If these special purpose men see you, they were some sort of intervention platoon," he said, "you'll be dead." I was very naive and I acted very naive during the war. I didn't think of hiding. But he took me aside. I didn't get the document on that day. I was told to go home and come back on the next day. I received this document, if you want to know, on the next day. On the next day I wanted to go, but a friend of mine advised me not to go to the MUP building alone. He volunteered to go with me because he knew Simo Drljaca personally. We went to see Simo Drljaca together and Simo received me. We talked. He was a very rough man, but he treated me quite decently. He didn't ignore me, as he did on previous occasions, and he issued this document, which said that I had been arrested by mistake and that after an investigation, it became clear that there was no reason to detain me any longer and that this was the reason for my release. I was also given another certificate which was permission to move around the town, because the Muslims in Prijedor had to have such permission, especially military-able men who were not in the army, but had other obligations. And to move around the town, they had to have a certificate issued by the secretariat of national defence or by the Ministry of the Interior. It varied. But usually it was the secretariat of national defence that issued these documents.
