We had to report there and be issued with these certificates, and in this way they knew how many of us there were in the town and who the people were who still remained in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What time does Your Honour want to break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think we can proceed for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, you mentioned that the document said an investigation had been done and you had been arrested by mistake. While you were in Omarska, was there any serious investigation or interrogation of you, concerning criminal allegations?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Every prisoner had to be interrogated. So my turn came as well. The circumstances were rather strange. I was questioned formally. It was simply a matter of form because I already knew that I was going home. So this was done simply as a matter of form. There were some questions, for example, they suspected that someone had taken medicines out of the hospital where I worked, and I was asked if I knew anything about this. And of course, I knew nothing about it. Then they asked me some questions about my private life. I know the investigator who interrogated me. His name was Drago Meakic. He was a relative of Zeljko Meakic I mentioned, and we had been in the reserve units of the army together, before I was a doctor. And he was a quartermaster, so we knew each other from the exercises then. And he knew me well. So I had the feeling that this was merely put up for show because they had to question me, but I had -- I didn't have the impression that they were actually accusing me or charging me with something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just so we're clear, this interrogation occurred after you were told by the camp commander you were released?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's what I said. It was after I found out that I was going home. That's when I was questioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a document that the witness -- or two documents that the witness has previously provided to the OTP. Copies have been made available to parties and the Chamber. May it be given a provisional number and shown to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: My understanding is they have no 65 ter numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So it's on the one and the same sheet of paper. Therefore, we should take only one number, and this would be S126B.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, first, can you explain briefly what these two documents are?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the title is "Permission to Move Around." It's issued by the Ministry of the Interior, and it even says here Sarajevo Security Services Centre, Banja Luka, public security station, Prijedor. This was issued to people who had to report to a certain place to be registered, and then to be given permission so that when they were stopped in the town by authorised officers, policemen, or whoever, they would be able to show it. This document issued by the security centre was given to me at the same time as the certificate saying I had been arrested by mistake and released from camp. The other document was issued by the Ministry of the Interior. You can see that the heading is different. And it's a form that had been printed earlier. The title is different. It's the "Ministry of Defence" and as a member of the Merhamet organisation, I was allowed to move around, and it even says that I was not to be mobilised or sent to work, under work obligation, like others. But rather, my obligation was to work in the Muslim charity organisation Merhamet. That was issued by Slavko Budimir, who was the head in that ministry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Beglerbegovic, could you please be so kind and read out both documents in toto.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'd be pleased to do that. "The Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Ministry of the Interior, Sarajevo. Security Services Centre in Banja Luka. Public security station in Prijedor. Number 11-12. Date:" And then it says 323. Permission to move around for Beglerbegovic, father's name Vehbija, Ibrahim. Allowing movement in the built-up area of Prijedor. (redacted) (redacted) That's my address. From the 24th of July, 1992, except during the curfew, from 2200 hours to 00.5 hours. This certificate shall be valid with an identity card or a passport. Chief of the public security station, Simo Drljaca." The other document, at the top it says in Cyrillic: "Not to be mobilised." That's some sort of signal that I was not to be sent to work anywhere else. And then it says: "Republika Srpska, the Ministry of Defence, Prijedor department, number 02-80-15/95. Date: The 22nd of September, 1995. Pursuant to Article 8 of the decree on the organisation and carrying out of work obligation, official gazette of Republika Srpska, number 8/92, the Ministry of Defence, Prijedor department, hereby issues the following certificate certifying that Beglerbegovic, father's name Vehbija, Ibrahim has been assigned to the municipal unit of work obligation, and that he is engaged in carrying out jobs according to the plan of the municipal Crisis Staff --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: -- Of the municipal staff of the civilian Defence in Prijedor. This certificate shall be issued in order to regulate the status of men liable for military service and will be valid until the 1st of November, 1995. Chief, Slavko Budimir."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Any objections against the admission into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, it has been wrongly translated. On page 49, line 8, it says "Crisis Staff" of the municipal staff. It doesn't say in this document. So I would like to read it so the translators can, first of all, correct it. It says: [Interpretation] "The municipal staff of the civil defence in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did apologise for making the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It just wasn't reflected in the record, Your Honour. It just seemed to read through on that line in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think now it's correct. What about the admission into evidence? Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do actually object to the document because it's broken down and it seems to be, although it's on one page identified as S126B, there's a middle portion that's in Cyrillic text. We would like to see the original and see what it came in the form. Secondly, we would like to object to the witness and no one laying a foundation on the signature of the individual. There seems to be three separate signatures, obviously we know there's three different individuals. The other objection on the second half involves a date that is beyond the dates of the indictment of April through September 1992. So we have an objection on relevance to that. Those would be our comments at this point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Before a decision, it seems to be appropriate that the Office of the Prosecutor goes into some details of this document, how the witness received the document and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And actually our interests is only the top document, but both are on one page. Your Honour, I think out of caution the address that was read out of the witness should be redacted from the transcript. It was on the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The address may be redacted. But possibly, the witness could explain -- once again, where and when precisely he received the first document under which circumstances, and whether or not he still has the original available.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, is it correct that this is a photocopy of two separate documents?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And were these documents, or this copy, given by you to some investigators from the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The two documents are obviously from two separate years. Is that correct? You received them on separate occasions?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. That's correct, yes. I don't know how it came about that both documents were photocopied on one sheet of paper. But the dates are different, and they were issued in different circumstances. The one on the top was issued in the summer of 1992 on my release from the camp when I was given the certificate of release from the camp. I was issued these two documents on the same day. The one on the bottom half of the page is in 1995, when I was already working in Merhamet, and that was my work obligation. So I did not have to go to the front line and perform my work obligation there. This was issued then. They have nothing to do with each other, these two documents, except that they are both issued in the same name. Their purpose was different. One was permission to move around the town, and the other is a certificate about my work obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: One question on the document regarding permission for movement, did you receive more than one of these documents during the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was in 1992, but on several occasions, I was called to report in a certain place because, as you can see, these documents have an expiry date, and then a new one has to be issued. I think the purpose was to count us and to have a register of all the people in Prijedor. All the documents were issued for only rather short periods of time. And the form of the documents differed. Sometimes they were small cards. Sometimes there was a printed form like this one. And they were issued on several occasions, but I can't remember at what intervals. His Honour asked me, and I can tell you that I do have the originals but I didn't bring them with me. I didn't think it was necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But it is your testimony that the original where we can see now photocopy of only the first part of the document, that was a document permission to move around, that you got and had to carry along with you. Right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then, this, only the second -- only the first part of the document, the permission to move around, is admitted into evidence as S126B.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, after your release -- does Your Honour want me to proceed, or would you like to take the break? Doctor, after your release, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: When I was released from the camp and given this piece of paper saying that I had been arrested by mistake and that there was no reason to investigate me any further, I felt safer somehow because I felt as if I had passed some sort of test and that I was no longer going to be persecuted. So I remained in Prijedor, even though with hindsight I see that my decision was very naive. However, fortunately, it ended well. The time I had spent in Omarska, well, I thought that was over. It was all over. But it wasn't like that. I did survive, however. But at any time, anyone could have entered my house, killed me, or looted the house. However, at the time, I naively trusted that everything was all right now and that this paper was a sort of guarantee that I could remain in Prijedor and go on living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Were you able to work, or did you stay at home?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't able to work. As I told you, on the 1st of July, I was dismissed from work, and I didn't work any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When did you begin working for Merhamet?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: It was in 1994 when I managed to send my two sons out of Prijedor. I managed to send them to Croatia with a convoy from Banja Luka. Even before that, there had been pressure from the representatives of Merhamet in Banja Luka for me to start work as a doctor, because the Muslims in Prijedor had no one to go to. The existing institutions, if they -- very often they were not treated well or provided with adequate service or they were afraid to leave their houses. There was, therefore, an initiative to provide health care for them through this charity organisation. There were several nurses there. I was one of the few doctors left in Prijedor. There were also two other doctors who were women, but they were afraid to move around because they had small children whom they didn't want to leave. And I was under pressure to start working as a doctor in Merhamet. I had two sons going to school. And Merhamet was not viewed with favour by the existing authorities. However, it was established, because of pressure from international organisations. The people working in Merhamet were somehow marked, and I was afraid that my children might suffer some consequences. That's why I did not join Merhamet until I had sent my children away. When they went to Croatia, I was less afraid. And then I joined Merhamet. That was in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Is it an appropriate time for a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stands adjourned until 5.40.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, you mentioned you worked for Merhamet in 1994. I want to cover this briefly. In 1995, were you arrested while working for Merhamet?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. In 1995, I think in January, I was in a convoy headed for Zagreb to get food for the Merhamet and medicine for the medical department of the Merhamet, for the medical unit. There were four freight vehicles with Merhamet officials. We went to Zagreb. And on the way back from Zagreb, I think we were around seven people. As soon as we got home, I only had enough time to take a shower before I was taken away by the police and taken to the MUP building in Prijedor. As the duty officer told us, this had been ordered by Simo Drljaca. No one asked us any questions, nor were we interrogated for the whole night. We just spent the night in the hall of the police building, the police station in Prijedor. The next day at 7.00 in the morning, Simo Drljaca came to work. He looked at us because he knew me. He just gave me a fleeting look, and then he walked upstairs. We stayed where we were. People, police officials, were coming to work. People came to get certificates and different documents issued. Our presence there was not really conspicuous because we might as well have been one of those people who came there to get documents. Around 11.00 Simo Drljaca came down the stairs from his office, and he saw me sitting opposite him. And he spoke to me. I was sitting there. He said: "What are you doing here? What are you waiting for?" I shrugged my shoulders and I said: "I don't even know myself." After a while, I'm not sure whether it was due to his intervention, he entered the room where the other police officers were. We were released and free to go home. Only Adil Solo stayed in the police station and the rest of us were released after 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Was that Adil Solo who was the vice-president, I believe, of Merhamet?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was the vice-president of the Merhamet and an activist, too. He is also a religious official. He is a hodza, as we call them. So he was there in his capacity as a hodza also.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you leave Prijedor municipality later that year, in 1995? And can you briefly describe the circumstances that led to you leaving Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In 1995, in October, in early October of 1995, I was forced to leave Prijedor. It was not of my own free will. I was expelled from my house. At 3.30 in the morning, the police came knocking. They were wearing Republika Srpska police uniforms. I knew two of the policemen who came. One of them was called Mudrinijic, and the other was Zoran Milojica. I don't know his first name. There were two other police officers with them. I think they were police officers. But probably from towns that had been liberated by the BH Army. Perhaps Petrovac or Kljuc or another town like that. They all came to Prijedor after that. There was a large number of refugees from Petrovac, Kljuc, in Prijedor. And among these refugees, there were some police officers. We were given half an hour to pack. And as the police officer put it we would be free to go to a democracy, as he said. I'm not sure what he meant. My wife was with me, and my mother, too, as well as my wife's parents, her father and mother. We packed whatever we could, in the brief time that we had been given. There was a van waiting outside the building. We were taken to a huge parking lot outside the town's stadium in Prijedor. We stayed until the next day at 3.00 in the afternoon. Occasionally, other people who were deported like us would arrive there. But in the afternoon hours, there was also a large number of people who had applied to the ICRC to leave Prijedor, to the Red Cross. But there Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. was some sort of a bottleneck there, so there were lots of people who wanted to leave but couldn't leave. And there were people who wanted to leave and applied to leave, and those who were not willing to leave but were deported and expelled. The convoy was set up around 3.00 in the afternoon and set out for Banja Luka. We reached Banja Luka and set out down the road across Borje. It's the name of a mountain, in the direction of Teslic. We stopped a couple of times along the road. We were advised not to leave the bus, not to show ourselves outside. Every bus was escorted. There were persons who were escorting each of the buses who were in charge of seeing to it that no one left the buses when the buses stopped. We reached Teslic. Again, the buses were shut. Again, the waiting. The escort person would leave the bus. They probably went out to have dinner, because it was getting dark. We spent more than one hour there, and we didn't know where we were going or what we could do. Then we drove down mountain roads for an hour maybe. We passed by a building with many police officers in it that must have been some sort of a forward command post or some sort of a police station on the ground. We stopped there, too. They came in and out. And then we continued very briefly, and then the bus was stopped again and we were ordered to leave the bus and take our things with us and to walk from there on. The path we took led first past a group of policemen who happened to be there. They were arrogant. They yelled at us. They had no scruples. They took our bags. They asked for money. They would take a young girl and start taking her towards the woods in full view of her parents, threatening them. In these cases, the parents would obviously give away whatever money they had left. A man walked up to me. He obviously saw that I was quite a stout and strong man, and he told me: "You're good for digging the trenches. We're not letting you go. But if you give me a hundred deutschmarks we will let you go." Of course, I did have that and I gave it to him. Even if he had asked for a thousand deutschmarks I would have given it to him. I used to joke later on that he was quite cheap, so he let me go. I carried my mother's luggage and my wife's luggage and everyone's luggage, and we passed a makeshift bridge. It was put together with planks. So even in a normal situation, a healthy strong man should be careful when crossing that sort of bridge. And it was dark, and it was slippery. So some people fell down from the makeshift bridge into the creek, and then got up to continue walking. My wife's relative hurt his knee because he hit his knee against something there, and the injury was so bad that he ended up in a hospital. There was another thing. One of the things they made us do was take off our watches. It's some sort of a routine thing, but the watch comes off easily because when someone takes it from you, you don't even notice. And they took all our packages and parcels. They just heaped them on one side of the road and said they would look through them later. And they blocked the road and told us: "On one side there is the creek. The other side of the road is mine, so you can't go there." And then they laid an obstacle across the road. It was a big -- it was not really a piece of wood or a branch. It was the whole limb of a tree placed on the road so that the branches faced in the direction of the creek and the narrow part was pointing to the hill. So you needed to be very physically able to get past it with all the luggage you were carrying on your back. When I managed to get across it, there was an elderly woman from Prijedor who had both her legs amputated at her hips. So she was also made to face an obstacle like this. And there was no way she could bend or be physically able enough to get past this sort of obstacle. So we helped her and carried her to get her across. So there were other cases like this. The path we had to walk was muddy from the rain or from humidity. It was soft mud. Everyone's shoes were wet. Everyone was soaking wet, and we continued for about seven or eight kilometres until we reached the BH Army positions where we were received and transported further on by buses and by cars. Some were taken to Travnik. Some to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Going back to 1992 after you were released from Omarska, during the time in 1992 that you spent at your house, did you ever hear any explosions?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. They were quite frequent explosions, especially at night. Not so much during the day. But as soon as it would get dark, there were explosions until early in the morning. It was quite strange if there weren't any explosions during the night. There was a shell almost every night, hitting one of the houses or the buildings there. Some cars were shelled, too, but I can't really say that there were many cars around because all the Muslim cars were taken, had been taken from their owners. Mostly Muslim houses were attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So you were able to determine when you saw the houses the next day that these were houses that had belonged to Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We knew it. Those were neighbours. It was clear that those were mostly Muslim houses. And this was one of the ways to put pressure on people to leave their houses, to go away. Those whose houses were damaged had to leave, and the neighbours of that person would just also leave because they were afraid. So if only one street was shelled, several families would immediately leave their street for fear that the same thing might happen to them, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you see any mosques or churches destroyed in Prijedor during 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. All the mosques in the Prijedor town area were destroyed. The mosque at Puharska. My part of town is also territorially part of that district, in terms of religious services. It was pulled down in late August. That was on the same day as an orthodox holiday. They call it Gospojna. Velika and Mala Gospojna. I'm not sure which holiday that was. Although I do know the Orthodox saints. I do know about them, but I can't remember. About five minutes after the mosque in Puharska had been destroyed, a Catholic church nearby in Prijedor was also destroyed. That is -- that was perhaps a hundred metres from my house. The mosque was not much further either, but it was a bit further away than the church. There were explosions all around. So many of the surrounding houses were destroyed, the windows were broken, smashed. So when the mosque was destroyed, the adjacent house was destroyed by the same explosion. And a husband and wife who spent the night in that house were killed on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do have a map that was prepared by my office that I'd like, at this time, to show to the witness. I would indicate that this shows certain religious institutions that are named in our indictment, and they are numbered. The pictures are numbered according to the numbers in our indictment. I think for purposes of proof, it will be very helpful to all the parties to have this particular document to understand which institutions we're talking about and how they relate to the particular institution enumerated in the indictment. So the Roman numerals on the photographs are the same Roman numerals that appear on the paragraph of religious destruction in the indictment. I would like, with Your Honours' permission, to ask this witness to look at the photographs number 10 and 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May we first of all, for the record, have this document as provisional 127.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If the Defence doesn't have a copy, they can have mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We do have. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, I'd just like you to look at photographs number 10 and 11. Do you recognise -- tell me if you can or cannot recognise the areas depicted. I'm talking about the upper right of the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Marked with Roman number 10?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. First number 10.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Here, you can only see the area where the church used to be, but I can't see the church there. There was a church there, but it was destroyed. And number 11 was also a place. It's still the same. There are only the ruins of the Puharska mosque that was destroyed. What I just told you about. But where the Catholic church used to be, there's nothing there now. I know Prijedor well enough to say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Is it correct that those two photographs, 10 and 11 that you just talked about, are the same church and mosque that you referred to earlier in your testimony as being destroyed? Is that correct, or not?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you aware if there was a mosque in Stari Grad before the conflict?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you see that mosque or see Stari Grad after May 30th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Not immediately after, because I couldn't move about that area. It was only later that I had a chance to see. But at the moment, when it was destroyed, and for a brief period of time immediately after that period, I couldn't see it just because I couldn't access the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Was that mosque in Stari Grad destroyed in 1992, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you see the area where that mosque was depicted in any of the photographs, and if so, can you tell us the number on the photograph? And if you're unsure, please tell us that.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sure. It's photograph number 6. You could see -- you can see there an empty meadow where the mosque used to be. And in the background, you can see houses that have been reconstructed. But without these houses, it would be difficult to say really because it's just a meadow. But the houses that are being built there now prove that this indeed is the scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm finished with that diagram.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, I'm interested whether you were aware of other crimes that were occurring in Prijedor without people being arrested or any investigation? Were you aware of people committing crimes openly without being arrested or punished for those crimes?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were cases where crimes had been committed, but the perpetrators were not identified. And there were other cases where, as you have said, crimes had been openly committed. And everyone knew who it had been, but the perpetrator was never punished.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you hear about a particular crime that occurred in the hospital that was widely discussed?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. At the hospital, one of these perpetrators broke into the hospital and there was a doctor who was carrying out an operation on an injured man. And this man who broke in came into the hospital following the man who was operated and killed this person on the surgical table. We are talking about a man called Zigic. And the doctor who was in charge was Mirza Bresic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know the ethnicity of the person who was killed on the operating table?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: He was a Muslim. He was an accomplice of the perpetrator. They Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. were both taxi drivers. His name was Omer Karadzic. They used to work together for a while, driving taxis. And for some reason Zigic found it necessary to try to kill him outside his own house. But when he failed and when they took the injured man to the hospital, he finished the job in the hospital. As far as I know, he was never punished. He just continued to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: After you were released from the Omarska camp, did you ever learn through other people that Dr. Stakic had been talking about how you were released?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. From a source I would not like to name, I found out that in some quarters, Dr. Stakic said that I had offered a bribe of 50.000 German mark to someone in the Omarska camp, and that was the reason why I had been released. First of all, I never gave this sort of money to anyone. And secondly, I don't know what the point of the whole story about the bribe was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: While you were in the Omarska camp, Doctor, did you see other colleagues, medical professionals, that you knew?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. There were a number of my colleagues in the Omarska camp. I have already referred to Dr. Esad Sadikovic, a throat, nose, and ear specialist. I contacted him when we were both in the camp. He even proposed, having realised that I was respected and privileged in some way by the guards, that they were not expecting the same sort of behaviour from me as they did from the others, he proposed to me that the two of us should freely visit all the different sections of the camp and offer medical assistance to those who were injured. This request or plan was never carried out because I was released in the meantime. Another doctor I saw there was Dr. Osman Mahmuljin, a man I was surprised to see in such bad shape. He was the quartermaster's assistant in the hospital. When the situation was still normal, he was a strong man, slightly conceited, perhaps I should even say arrogant. He always emphasised his own alleged superiority over everyone else, including me. But when I saw him in the camp, he spoke to me as if addressing a parent. He complained about some banality. He told me: "Ibro, I'm running a fever. I'm sick. I need help." And his voice was that of a small child, talking to a parent, asking for help. I knew this man. I felt his skin, and I said: "Well, you're not running a fever." His arm had been broken, and he probably had been tortured, so the way he felt was probably a consequence of the treatment that he had undergone. There was also Dr. Esad [as interpreted] Begic there. I didn't know him so well as the first two I've mentioned. There was also Dr. Rufad Suljanovic, a general practitioner. There was Dr. Habiba Harambasic, called Biba, the dentist. So she was a woman inmate. There was Dr. Sead Curak. My colleague. Then there was also earlier Dr. Zeljko Sikora, a Croat by nationality, a physiologist. There is Dr. Jusuf Pasic, a general practitioner from Kozarac who had worked for many years in Kozarac. He was a living legend respected by everyone, not only people from Kozarac, but also Serbs who lived in the area. He was their favorite doctor. I'm not sure that's all, but that's more or less what I could say about the doctors I saw in the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just to clarify, the name of Dr. Begic, his first name, is Esad or Enes?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Enes. Enes. It could either be Enes or Enez, and as far as I know his first name was Enez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And forgive me, but did you mention Dr. Rufad Suljanovic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Rufad Suljanovic. Yes, I did mention him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, can you tell us what you know about the fate of Dr. Esad Sadikovic, Osman Mahmuljin, Zeljko Sikora, Enez Begic, Jusuf Pasic, and Rufad Suljanovic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I know that they are not around, that they never came out of the camp and they are not alive. But what exactly happened to them, I couldn't say. I can't say anything about the precise circumstances of their death.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You told us earlier that the medical community in Prijedor was intermingled and they knew each other. Based upon your knowledge of the medical community, do you believe that Dr. Stakic was familiar or knew any of these individuals that you've just named?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I think he knew most of them. I don't know about all of them. He would know that. But working in Prijedor and in Omarska and having the usual kinds of contacts, I think he would have known most of those doctors, especially Sadikovic, Mahmuljin, and probably Dr. Jusuf Pasic because they were specialists, and Dr. Pasic worked in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor, for your testimony. One final question: You've mentioned several times that you felt -- you feel now that you were somewhat naive back in 1992 when these events were occurring. Looking back now ten years later, can you tell us your impression of whether these events that you witnessed were random events or whether you believe now that they were part of a broader policy or plan?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we believe that this is speculation. So we object to this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think if the question could be rephrased and include the question whether or not there is a certain knowledge and basis of facts for an answer, that would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Let me try to rephrase it and Your Honour can tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, can you tell us now why you believe you were naive in 1992? What has happened, or what are you aware of, that makes you think now that you were naive back then?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BEGLERBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the fact -- I already said at the beginning that when overnight there was this peaceful takeover in Prijedor, I thought that it was something that had taken place in the heads of a group of ambitious people and that it would not last long. Even when the second event happened, I thought, "well, this is an isolated event." It's something perpetrated by a small group of people. However, as time went by, when things happen and you see that they are terrible and you think they can't get any worse, and then they do get worse, you see that it's not accidental, that it's not happening by chance, that it's part of a plan that was drawn up somewhere and that is being gradually implemented step by step, that a plan must have been drawn up somewhere and that it was being implemented in various places and in various regions because if you look at the way things happened, the Serbian autonomous regions that were set up, and then there were attempts in the Prijedor itself on one occasion, to publish a map dividing the town into a Serbian part and a Muslim part which was unimaginable because there was simply no border like that. But later on, it turned out that all of Bosnia was being divided in this way. So all this led me to conclude that this was a premeditated overall plan that was being implemented on the ground. They were looking for excuses to start a conflict. Some sort of attacks were mounted, a scenario was created in several places. And all this leads me to conclude that none of it happened by chance. It's true that I was naive, as it turned out, I was the most afraid when I found myself in Sanski Most after the liberation when I looked back and saw what sort of dire straits I had been in and how I could have lost my head. It was only after the event. I don't know why I remained. It was probably a wish to live in my hometown and to preserve what I had. It could have cost me my life, but fortunately it didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: This concludes my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it the understanding that it would be better to start the cross-examination not today but tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We just wanted to propose the same thing to give Dr. Beglerbegovic a chance to rest until tomorrow. And we could sort out our questions to have a speedy cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. But we shouldn't conclude for today.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I do have one question, with the Court's permission. If I just may. Therefore, no admission into evidence of this document. May we then turn to that what was addressed in the beginning. We still have open some documents from our last witness, Witness Q. And I think it starts -- it started with S118. If you please, can recall what Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. document is what.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document S118 is the name sheet of Witness Q. And it has been admitted and marked confidential.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: S119, S120, and 121, these were the sketches drawn by Witness Q. Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, with the exception of one of them, we do not object. utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then we can start a more less difficult exercise for the remaining 20 minutes that we know what we have ahead us for tomorrow. Starting with list number 2, I hope everybody has this list available. It starts with which provisional number?

utterances.text: I believe that the first relevant one would be S207, when I reviewed this list.

utterances.text: I would say for not confusing, we should stay in the order of the list.

utterances.text: Do you have another list? Mine starts with 99.

utterances.text: You might have missed that one because it says "Crisis Staff signed" and I just want the Defence to be on notice that I believe that's the signature of the accused. It doesn't have his name printed below it, but the signature appears to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It has nothing to do. We come especially back to those documents we discussed this morning. I only want to try not to confuse this binder. And I do believe that the Prosecutor had something in mind when tendering this document, if you could please explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour is asking now do we want to move these into evidence?

utterances.text: I didn't come here prepared to talk about that. The documents on list 3, all of those --

utterances.text: List 2, I haven't actually -- list 2 in reviewing that, it actually was put together by somebody else on my team. utterances.text: Yes. We would definitely be moving that into evidence. It has been...

We object to that document as well. We would like to further question Mr. Inayat on some of these documents. I know he only provided us with limited testimony -- and it was my understanding he will be called back -- and just gave us an overview of how the mechanism behind the office of the investigator works. So based on that, we would object to the admission of that document.

utterances.text: Any remarks in favour of this document?

utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We do object to this document. This one certainly doesn't match his signature. It does not have his correct spelling of his name. It seems to just have his first name spelled, and this is one of many. And I could list out, if the Court wants, or we can just say, same objection, same basis. This is one of the examples that we found, and we found three to five various or seemingly various handwritings, although we're not handwriting experts either. There are some that we will confirm were that of Dr. Stakic, but this one in particular we have as with others an objection to on those grounds.

And this is also another example of how the signatures do not and are inconsistent on some of these documents. And this is yet a second example of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just that it's unsigned, Your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence, 67A and 67B. 219.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With respect to 219, Judge, we would adopt and incorporate our previous objection and bases that were given with respect to Exhibit Number S64 which had a 65 ter number of 207.

utterances.text: Yes. Observations by the OTP?

utterances.text: I think it's a highly relevant document, and it bears the name of the accused as the person authorising this order.

utterances.text: Same objection and same basis as outlined with respect to S68A and B and S64A and B, ter number 219 and ter number 207 respectfully. utterances.text: S81, which has the ter number 257.

utterances.text: Just to clarify. Is that the end of list 2? I have list 2 going through 92.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Until today, it's a package solution. And we have to take care. It's 7.01.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I do have one question of the Court, if I may, of the Court if you could just give us some guidance very quickly. We don't generally object to the principle of asking witnesses any questions. However, a witness who is designated as a fact witness, we think, should be prohibited from giving opinion testimony as we have just seen, or at least that I've seen here. By asking a witness - and I'm speaking quickly and I apologise - whether or not now his impressions have changed and whether or not it's a random or whether or not it is a widespread and systematic and something that is concrete, which are fundamental elements that only this Trial Chamber will conclude, I think it's unfair to the Defence. I think it raises numerous objections to us. I'm sorry. The witness, obviously being a gentleman and being a professional, we did not want and refrained from interrupting. I just want to know for the future if other fact witnesses will be transposed at the end of their testimony and become expert witnesses. And if that's the manner in which we're going to proceed, just that the same leeway, if you can call it that, be given also to the Defence, that we have fact witnesses that may or may not have been in the various detention centres or camps, and that they will be allowed to give expert, in essence, opinion testimony which is what this witness, I regrettably believe, gave. And I don't think it's his position to give it. I don't think he has the knowledge, the background, the information to give this Court that type of testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Also in the future, we will decided on a case-to-case basis. And indeed, we all, Judges included, should refrain in principle from these questions. But we have really to conclude for today. Thank you.
